l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 12
s: King Herod kills James, the brother of John, and arrests Peter during the days of unleavened bread, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover. While the assembly prays constantly, an angel of the Lord frees Peter from the prison, and Peter goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John called Mark. The servant girl Rhoda recognizes his voice but the gathered believers do not believe her until they open the gate and see him. Peter tells them to report to James and the brothers, then leaves. Herod has the guards put to death, and at Caesarea an angel of the Lord strikes him down after the crowd calls his speech the voice of a god; the word of God grows, and Barnabas and Saul return to Jerusalem with John called Mark.

l: King Herod, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 12
s: King Herod oppresses some of the assembly, kills James the brother of John with the sword, and arrests Peter, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover. After Peter escapes, Herod examines the guards and commands that they be put to death, then goes to Caesarea. There, angry with Tyre and Sidon, he gives a speech in royal clothing, accepts the crowd's cry that he is a god, and is struck by an angel of the Lord, eaten by worms, and dies because he did not give God the glory.

l: Peter, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 12
s: Peter is seized by Herod and held under guard by four squads of four soldiers, sleeping bound with two chains between two soldiers. An angel wakes him, his chains fall off, and he follows the angel past the guards and through the iron gate, at first thinking it is a vision. He then recognizes that the Lord delivered him, goes to Mary's house, tells the believers how the Lord brought him out, asks them to tell James and the brothers, and departs to another place.

l: angel of the Lord, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 12
s: An angel of the Lord appears in Peter's cell with a light, strikes Peter on the side to wake him, and tells him to get dressed, put on his sandals and cloak, and follow. He leads Peter past the first and second guard to the iron gate, which opens by itself, and departs after they go down one street. Later an angel of the Lord strikes Herod because he did not give God the glory.

l: disciples (believers gathered at Pentecost), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 12
s: The assembly is oppressed by Herod, who kills James and arrests Peter. While Peter is kept in prison, the assembly makes constant prayer to God for him. Many are gathered praying at Mary's house when Peter arrives, and they doubt Rhoda's report, saying it must be his angel, until they open the gate and are amazed to see him.

l: prison (where Peter was held), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 12
s: The prison is where Herod puts Peter under guard of four squads of four soldiers, with guards in front of the door. Peter is bound with two chains in the cell between two soldiers. He leaves it with the angel, passing the first and second guard and an iron gate that opens by itself, and the next morning the soldiers are in a stir over what became of him.

l: Rhoda, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 12
s: Rhoda is a servant girl who comes to answer when Peter knocks at the door of the gate at Mary's house. She recognizes his voice and, for joy, runs in to report that he is standing there without opening the gate. When told she is crazy, she insists it is so.

l: the Lord, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 12
s: The Lord is credited with sending out his angel and delivering Peter from the hand of Herod and from everything the Jewish people were expecting. Peter declares how the Lord brought him out of the prison. His angel strikes Herod, and the word of God grows and multiplies.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: In Chapter 13, the Holy Spirit directs the prophets and teachers at Antioch to separate Barnabas and Saul, who are sent out and sail to Cyprus with John as attendant. At Paphos, the sorcerer Elymas (Bar Jesus) opposes them before the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and Paul strikes him with blindness, after which the proconsul believes. John leaves them at Perga and returns to Jerusalem, while Paul and Barnabas go on to Antioch of Pisidia, where Paul preaches in the synagogue, tracing Israel's history to David and proclaiming Jesus' resurrection and forgiveness of sins. The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathers, the Jews contradict and blaspheme, and Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, many of whom believe. The Jews stir up a persecution that drives the two out, and they go to Iconium while the disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Also called Saul, Paul is separated with Barnabas by the Holy Spirit's direction, strikes the sorcerer Elymas with blindness at Paphos, and preaches in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. After Jewish opposition he and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, and are then thrown out of the region and go to Iconium.

l: Barnabas, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Barnabas, one of the prophets and teachers at Antioch, is set apart with Saul for the Spirit's work and travels with him to Cyprus and Antioch of Pisidia. He joins Paul in speaking boldly to the Jews and turning to the Gentiles, and is driven out with him before they go to Iconium.

l: Holy Spirit, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: The Holy Spirit speaks to the Antioch assembly, directing them to separate Barnabas and Saul for the work he has called them to, and sends them out. Paul is filled with the Spirit when he confronts Elymas, and at the end the disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: In Paul's sermon God is portrayed as the one who chose the fathers, led them out of Egypt, gave the land, judges, and kings, and raised up David. He fulfilled his promise by bringing salvation through Jesus and raising him from the dead.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Paul preaches that Jesus came from David's offspring as the promised savior, announced by John, and was condemned by the Jerusalem rulers though no cause for death was found. God raised him from the dead without decay, and through him forgiveness of sins and justification are proclaimed.

l: Antioch of Pisidia, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Paul and Barnabas arrive here from Perga and enter the synagogue on the Sabbath, where Paul preaches. The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathers to hear the word, but Jewish opposition and a persecution stirred up among prominent women and men lead to the missionaries' expulsion.

l: Elymas, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Elymas, also called Bar Jesus, is a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet attached to the proconsul at Paphos. He opposes Barnabas and Saul, trying to turn the proconsul from the faith, and Paul declares him a son of the devil and he is struck with blindness for a season.

l: Sergius Paulus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Sergius Paulus is the proconsul at Paphos, a man of understanding, who summons Barnabas and Saul to hear God's word. After seeing Elymas struck blind, he believes, astonished at the Lord's teaching.

l: Israel, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Paul's sermon recounts Israel's history: chosen fathers, deliverance from Egypt, forty years in the wilderness, the conquest of Canaan, judges, and the kings Saul and David. God brought salvation to Israel from David's offspring according to his promise, preceded by John's baptism of repentance to Israel.

l: David, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Paul says God raised David up as king after removing Saul and testified that he was a man after his heart who would do all his will. David died and saw decay, in contrast to Jesus, who was raised and did not, and the promised salvation came from his offspring.

l: Jews of Antioch of Pisidia, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Some Jews and devout proselytes follow Paul and Barnabas after the first sermon, but when the crowds gather the next Sabbath, the Jews are filled with jealousy, contradict Paul, and blaspheme. They stir up the devout and prominent women and chief men to persecute the missionaries and expel them.

l: Gentiles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: The Gentiles at Antioch beg to hear the words again the next Sabbath, and almost the whole city gathers. When Paul and Barnabas turn to them, they are glad, glorify the word of God, and those appointed to eternal life believe, spreading the word through the region.

l: Paul's sermon at Antioch of Pisidia, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: In the synagogue Paul addresses Men of Israel and God-fearers, surveying Israel's history from the exodus to David, then announcing John's testimony, Jesus' death, and God's raising of him. He cites the psalms, offers forgiveness and justification beyond the law of Moses, and warns scoffers with a prophetic quotation.

l: salvation and forgiveness through Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Paul proclaims that through Jesus remission of sins is announced, and everyone who believes is justified from all things from which the law of Moses could not justify. The word of this salvation is sent to Israel's children and God-fearers, and later to the Gentiles as a light to the ends of the earth.

l: resurrection of Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: Paul declares that God raised Jesus from the dead, that he was seen for many days by witnesses who came with him from Galilee, and that this fulfills the promise to the fathers. He supports it with psalm quotations and contrasts Jesus, who saw no decay, with David, who did.

l: Gentile mission, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 13
s: After the Holy Spirit sends out Barnabas and Saul, they proclaim the word first in synagogues, but at Antioch of Pisidia they declare that, since the Jews reject it, they turn to the Gentiles. They cite the Lord's command that they be a light for the Gentiles bringing salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas speak in the synagogue and many Jews and Greeks believe, but unbelieving Jews turn the Gentiles against them and the city divides. When a plot to stone them arises, they flee to Lystra and Derbe in Lycaonia and preach the Good News. At Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowd takes Barnabas and Paul for Jupiter and Mercury and a priest prepares to sacrifice to them, until the apostles tear their clothes and plead with the people to turn to the living God. Jews from Antioch and Iconium persuade the crowds, stone Paul and drag him out of the city, but he rises and goes on to Derbe. The two then revisit the cities, strengthen disciples, appoint elders, return to Antioch, and report that God had opened a door of faith to the nations.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: Paul speaks in Iconium, flees to Lystra, and heals a lame man there, after which he is called Mercury as chief speaker. He pleads with the crowd not to sacrifice to him, is then stoned and dragged out of Lystra as if dead, yet rises and goes to Derbe. He and Barnabas later strengthen disciples, appoint elders, and report back at Antioch.

l: Barnabas, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: Barnabas accompanies Paul in Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, and the Lystrans call him Jupiter. He tears his clothes with Paul to stop the sacrifice, then travels with Paul to appoint elders and returns to Antioch to report what God had done.

l: Iconium, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas speak in the synagogue and many Jews and Greeks believe, but the city becomes divided between Jews and apostles. A violent plot to mistreat and stone them forces them to flee. Jews from Iconium later help turn the Lystra crowds against Paul, and the apostles revisit Iconium to strengthen disciples.

l: Lystra, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: Lystra is a city of Lycaonia where the apostles flee and preach, and where a lame man is healed. The people there mistake the apostles for gods, and Paul is later stoned outside the city. Paul and Barnabas return to Lystra afterward to strengthen the disciples.

l: Jews (opponents of Paul and Barnabas), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: Unbelieving Jews in Iconium stir up the Gentiles against the brothers and join in a plot to mistreat and stone the apostles. Jews from Antioch and Iconium then come to Lystra, persuade the crowds, and stone Paul, dragging him out of the city.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: God testifies to the word of his grace by granting signs and wonders through the apostles' hands. Paul describes him as the living God who made the sky, earth, sea, and all in them, who allowed nations to walk their own ways yet left witness through rains and fruitful seasons. The apostles report that he opened a door of faith to the nations.

l: crowd of Lystra (multitude at Lystra), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: After seeing the healing, the crowd cries out in the Lycaonian language that the gods have come down in the likeness of men. They call Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury, and with their priest they nearly sacrifice to them, being hardly restrained. Persuaded by Jews from Antioch and Iconium, they then join in stoning Paul.

l: lame man (man at Lystra), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: A man at Lystra, crippled in his feet from his mother's womb and never having walked, listens to Paul speak. Paul sees that he has faith to be made whole and tells him to stand upright, and he leaps up and walks.

l: healing of the lame man, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: Paul, seeing the man's faith, commands him with a loud voice to stand upright, and the man leaps up and walks. The miracle leads the Lystra crowd to take the apostles for gods and attempt a sacrifice to them.

l: stoning of Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: Jews from Antioch and Iconium persuade the Lystra crowds, who stone Paul and drag him out of the city, supposing him dead. As disciples stand around him, he rises, re-enters the city, and the next day leaves with Barnabas for Derbe.

l: Good News, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 14
s: The apostles preach the Good News in Lystra and Derbe after fleeing Iconium, and make many disciples in Derbe. Paul tells the Lystrans that the Good News calls them to turn from vain things to the living God.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: Men from Judea teach that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved, which causes discord with Paul and Barnabas in Antioch. Paul, Barnabas, and others are sent to Jerusalem, where some believing Pharisees insist on circumcision and keeping the law of Moses. Peter argues that God gave the Gentiles the Holy Spirit and saved them by grace, and James proposes that only a few things be asked of them: abstaining from idol pollution, sexual immorality, strangled meat, and blood. The apostles, elders, and assembly send a letter with Judas Barsabbas and Silas to Antioch, where it is read with rejoicing. Afterward Paul and Barnabas quarrel over taking Mark, and separate: Barnabas sails to Cyprus with Mark, while Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: Paul disputes with the men from Judea in Antioch and is appointed to go to Jerusalem, where he reports what God did among the Gentiles. Later he refuses to take Mark, whom he says withdrew in Pamphylia, so he separates from Barnabas, chooses Silas, and travels through Syria and Cilicia strengthening the assemblies.

l: Barnabas, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: Barnabas goes with Paul to Jerusalem and reports signs and wonders among the nations. He later wants to take John Mark on a return visit, and after a sharp contention with Paul he sails to Cyprus with Mark.

l: Peter, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: Peter speaks at the Jerusalem gathering, saying God chose that the nations hear the Good News through his mouth and gave the Gentiles the Holy Spirit just as to the Jewish believers. He calls the law a yoke neither the fathers nor they could bear and says all are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus.

l: James, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: James speaks after Peter, citing Simeon's report and the words of the prophets about rebuilding David's tabernacle so the Gentiles may seek the Lord. He gives his judgment that Gentile turners to God not be troubled, but be told to abstain from idol pollution, sexual immorality, strangled meat, and blood.

l: Silas, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: Silas, with Judas called Barsabbas, is chosen as a chief man among the brothers to carry the letter to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas and to confirm it by word of mouth. He, as a prophet, encourages and strengthens the brothers, and later Paul chooses him as his companion when he leaves Antioch.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: God is said to have chosen Peter's mouth for the Gentiles to hear the Good News, and to have testified to them by giving the Holy Spirit and cleansing their hearts by faith. He did signs and wonders among the nations through Paul and Barnabas, and his works are known to him from eternity.

l: Jerusalem, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: Jerusalem is where Paul, Barnabas, and others go to bring the circumcision question to the apostles and elders. It is the place where the assembly receives them, the matter is debated, and the decision and letter originate.

l: Antioch, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: Antioch is where the dispute over circumcision arises and where the letter is delivered and read to the gathered multitude, who rejoice. Paul and Barnabas remain there teaching, and it is from there that Paul and Barnabas part ways.

l: Gentiles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: The Gentiles are said to have turned to God and received the Holy Spirit, and their conversion brings great joy to the brothers. The council decides not to trouble them with circumcision, asking only that they keep a few necessary things.

l: men from Judea, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: Some men came down from Judea teaching the brothers that without circumcision after Moses' custom they could not be saved. The Jerusalem letter says they went out from the apostles and elders without any commandment and troubled and unsettled the Gentile believers' souls.

l: apostles and elders, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: The apostles and elders receive Paul and Barnabas in Jerusalem and gather to examine the matter. They, with the whole assembly, choose men to send to Antioch and write the letter, stating it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them to lay no greater burden.

l: circumcision requirement, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: The claim that circumcision after Moses' custom is necessary for salvation is taught by the men from Judea and urged by believing Pharisees. It is rejected in the council's outcome, which lays no such burden on Gentile believers.

l: law of Moses, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: Some believing Pharisees say Gentiles must be commanded to keep the law of Moses. James notes that Moses has long been preached in every city and read in the synagogues each Sabbath, while the council declines to impose the law on Gentile believers.

l: Jerusalem council, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: The apostles and elders gather after much discussion, hearing Peter, Barnabas and Paul, and James. They reach one accord that Gentile believers should not be burdened beyond a few necessary things and decide to send a letter.

l: letter to Gentile believers, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: The letter is written by the apostles, elders, and brothers to Gentile brothers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia, disowning those who troubled them and stating the necessary things. It is carried by Judas and Silas with Paul and Barnabas, and read in Antioch, where the people rejoice at its encouragement.

l: necessary things (Gentile requirements), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 15
s: The requirements are to abstain from things sacrificed to idols, blood, things strangled, and sexual immorality. The letter says that if they keep themselves from these, it will be well with them.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: Paul travels through Derbe and Lystra, where he circumcises Timothy, a disciple well spoken of by the brothers, and takes him along while delivering the Jerusalem decrees to the cities. The Holy Spirit forbids them to speak in Asia and disallows entry into Bithynia, and at Troas Paul sees a vision of a Macedonian man begging for help, so the company goes to Macedonia. At Philippi, Lydia, a seller of purple from Thyatira, listens, is baptized with her household, and hosts them. After Paul casts a spirit of divination out of a girl, her masters drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed. An earthquake opens the prison, the jailer and his household believe and are baptized, and the next day Paul objects that he and Silas are Romans, so the frightened magistrates plead with them to leave the city, and they visit Lydia's house and the brothers before departing.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: Paul has Timothy circumcised and take part in the journey, and he receives a vision at Troas of a man of Macedonia asking for help. At Philippi he commands a spirit out of a girl, is beaten and jailed with Silas, tells the jailer to believe in the Lord Jesus, and insists that the magistrates come themselves to release him because he is a Roman.

l: Silas, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: Silas is seized with Paul, dragged before the rulers, beaten with rods, and put in the inner prison with his feet in stocks. At midnight he prays and sings hymns with Paul, and he hears the word spoken to the jailer's household.

l: Timothy, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: Timothy is a disciple at Lystra, the son of a believing Jewess and a Greek father, and the brothers at Lystra and Iconium speak well of him. Paul wants him to go along and circumcises him because of the Jews in those parts who knew his father was a Greek.

l: Lydia, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: Lydia is a seller of purple from Thyatira who worships God, and the Lord opens her heart to Paul's words at the riverside. She and her household are baptized, and she persuades the company to stay in her house, where they later return and meet the brothers.

l: jailer, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: The jailer puts Paul and Silas in the inner prison with their feet in stocks, and when the earthquake opens the doors he nearly kills himself until Paul calls out. He asks what he must do to be saved, hears the word, washes their stripes, is baptized with his household, and rejoices having believed in God.

l: girl with a spirit of divination, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: The girl, who earns much gain for her masters by fortune telling, follows Paul and the others for many days crying out that they are servants of the Most High God proclaiming a way of salvation. Paul commands the spirit to come out of her in the name of Jesus Christ, and it leaves at that hour.

l: girl's masters, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: When the spirit is gone, the masters see that the hope of their gain is lost and seize Paul and Silas. They drag them before the rulers and accuse them of agitating the city as Jews and advocating customs unlawful for Romans.

l: magistrates, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: The magistrates tear the clothes from Paul and Silas and order them beaten with rods and jailed. The next day they send sergeants to release them, but they become afraid on learning the two are Romans, and they come, beg them, bring them out, and ask them to leave the city.

l: Macedonia, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: Macedonia is the region from which a man in Paul's night vision begs him to come over and help. Concluding the Lord has called them to preach the Good News there, the company sails to Neapolis and on to Philippi.

l: Philippi, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: Philippi is described as a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, and a Roman colony, where the company stays some days. There Lydia and her household are baptized, the girl is freed of her spirit, and Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned before leaving.

l: prison, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: The prison holds Paul and Silas in its inner part with their feet in stocks, while other prisoners listen to their hymns. At midnight its foundations shake and its doors open, and afterward Paul and Silas leave it and go to Lydia's house.

l: earthquake, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: A great earthquake strikes about midnight while Paul and Silas pray and sing, shaking the prison's foundations. All the doors open and everyone's bonds are loosened, which leads the jailer to draw his sword and then to ask how to be saved.

l: beating of Paul and Silas, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 16
s: The magistrates, with the multitude rising against them, have Paul and Silas's clothes torn off and order them beaten with rods, laying many stripes on them before the prison. Paul later protests that it was done publicly and without a trial to men who are Romans, which frightens the magistrates.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Paul and Silas travel through Amphipolis and Apollonia to Thessalonica, where Paul reasons from the Scriptures in the synagogue for three Sabbaths and some Jews, many devout Greeks, and prominent women believe. The unpersuaded Jews stir up a mob, attack Jason's house, and drag Jason and other brothers before the city rulers, who take security and release them. Paul and Silas are sent by night to Beroea, where the Jews examine the Scriptures daily and many believe, until Jews from Thessalonica arrive and agitate the crowds. Paul is escorted to Athens while Silas and Timothy remain behind. In Athens, provoked by the idols, Paul debates in the synagogue and marketplace and is brought before the Areopagus by Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, where he speaks about the unknown God, repentance, and the resurrection, with mixed responses and a few believers including Dionysius and Damaris.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Paul came to Thessalonica and reasoned from the Scriptures in the synagogue for three Sabbaths, proclaiming that Jesus is the Christ who had to suffer and rise. Driven out by a mob, he went to Beroea, then was escorted to Athens, where he was provoked by the idols, debated in the synagogue and marketplace, and spoke at the Areopagus. Some mocked him, some wanted to hear more, and a few believed.

l: Silas, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Silas joined Paul in Thessalonica, where some were persuaded and joined him and Paul. He was sent with Paul by night to Beroea and stayed there with Timothy when Paul was sent on toward the sea. Paul sent a commandment for Silas and Timothy to come to him in Athens very quickly.

l: Thessalonica, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Thessalonica had a Jewish synagogue where Paul reasoned for three Sabbaths; some Jews, a great multitude of devout Greeks and many chief women joined him. Unpersuaded Jews raised a mob and brought Jason and other brothers before the city rulers, who were troubled and took security from them. The Beroeans are described as more noble than those in Thessalonica.

l: Beroea, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Paul and Silas were sent there by night and went into the Jewish synagogue. The people received the word with readiness and examined the Scriptures daily, and many Jews, prominent Greek women and not a few men believed. Jews from Thessalonica came and agitated the crowds, so Paul was sent away.

l: Athens, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Paul was brought to Athens by his escorts and waited there for Silas and Timothy. He was provoked at seeing the city full of idols and reasoned in the synagogue and daily in the marketplace. The Athenians and resident strangers are said to spend their time only telling or hearing something new.

l: Areopagus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Philosophers took Paul to the Areopagus, asking to know what his new teaching was. Paul stood in its middle and gave his speech there. Dionysius the Areopagite was among those who joined Paul and believed.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Paul proclaimed that Jesus is the Christ who had to suffer and rise from the dead. In Thessalonica his accusers charged that Jesus was another king contrary to Caesar's decrees. In Athens, Paul's preaching of Jesus and the resurrection led some to think he advocated foreign deities, and he said God will judge the world by a man he ordained and raised from the dead.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: In Paul's Areopagus speech, God is the maker of the world and Lord of heaven and earth, who does not dwell in hand-made temples or need human service, and who gives all life and breath. He determined the nations' seasons and boundaries so people would seek him, overlooked the times of ignorance, now commands all to repent, and has appointed a day of judgment, giving assurance by raising the man he ordained from the dead.

l: Jews of Thessalonica, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: The unpersuaded Jews took wicked men from the marketplace, gathered a crowd and set the city in an uproar, assaulting Jason's house and dragging Jason and others before the rulers. They accused Paul's group of turning the world upside down and acting against Caesar's decrees. When they learned Paul was preaching in Beroea, they went there and agitated the multitudes.

l: Beroean Jews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: The Jews at Beroea are called more noble than those in Thessalonica because they received the word with all readiness and examined the Scriptures daily to check Paul's claims. As a result many of them believed.

l: Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers conversed with Paul in Athens. Some called him a babbler, others said he seemed to advocate foreign deities because he preached Jesus and the resurrection. They took him to the Areopagus to explain his new teaching.

l: Athenians, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Paul told the Athenians they were very religious, citing an altar inscribed 'TO AN UNKNOWN GOD'. The text says the Athenians and resident strangers spent their time only telling or hearing new things. After the speech some mocked at the resurrection, others wanted to hear more, and some, including Dionysius and Damaris, believed.

l: Paul's speech at the Areopagus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 17
s: Paul began from the altar to an unknown God and declared that the God who made the world does not dwell in temples or need human service. He said God made every nation from one blood to seek him, quoted poets that 'we are also his offspring', argued that the Divine Nature is not like gold, silver or stone, and called all people to repent because of a coming judgment by a man God raised from the dead. Reaction was divided between mockery and a wish to hear more, and some believed.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: Paul leaves Athens for Corinth, where he lives and works with the tent makers Aquila and Priscilla, who had left Rome under Claudius's order. He reasons in the synagogue, and when the Jews oppose him he turns to the Gentiles, staying in Justus's house; Crispus and many Corinthians believe, and the Lord encourages him in a vision. The Jews bring Paul before the proconsul Gallio, who refuses to judge a dispute about their law, drives them off, and ignores the beating of Sosthenes by the Greeks. Paul then sails with Priscilla and Aquila to Ephesus, leaves them there, goes on to Caesarea, Antioch, and Galatia and Phrygia. Meanwhile Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian Jew, comes to Ephesus, is taught more accurately by Priscilla and Aquila, and goes on to Achaia, where he refutes the Jews from the Scriptures.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: Paul leaves Athens for Corinth, works as a tent maker with Aquila and Priscilla, and reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath. After the Jews oppose him he declares he will go to the Gentiles, stays a year and six months teaching, and is encouraged by the Lord in a vision. He is brought before Gallio, then shaves his head at Cenchreae for a vow, sails with Priscilla and Aquila, leaves them at Ephesus, promises to return if God wills, and travels via Caesarea and Antioch through Galatia and Phrygia strengthening disciples.

l: Aquila, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: Aquila is a Jew from Pontus who recently came from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius ordered the Jews out of Rome. He shares Paul's tent-making trade and hosts him, then sails with Paul and is left at Ephesus. There he and Priscilla take Apollos aside and explain the way of God to him more accurately.

l: Priscilla, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: Priscilla is the wife of Aquila, who came from Italy after Claudius's expulsion of the Jews from Rome and works as a tent maker. She travels with Paul and Aquila to Ephesus and stays there. She and Aquila explain the way of God more accurately to Apollos.

l: Apollos, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: Apollos is a Jew from Alexandria, eloquent and mighty in the Scriptures, who comes to Ephesus. He teaches accurately about Jesus though he knows only John's baptism, and Priscilla and Aquila take him aside to teach him more fully. Encouraged by the brothers, who write to the disciples in Achaia, he goes there, helps believers, and publicly refutes the Jews from the Scriptures showing that Jesus is the Christ.

l: Gallio, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: Gallio is proconsul of Achaia when the Jews bring Paul before his judgment seat. Before Paul can speak, he rules that questions about words, names, and the Jews' own law are not his concern and drives them from the seat. He pays no attention when the Greeks beat Sosthenes in front of him.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: Paul testifies to the Jews at Corinth that Jesus is the Christ. Apollos teaches accurately about Jesus, though knowing only John's baptism, and later shows publicly from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

l: Jews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: At Corinth, the Jews oppose and blaspheme when Paul testifies that Jesus is the Christ, so he turns to the Gentiles. They rise up together against Paul and bring him before Gallio, who sends them away. At Ephesus they ask Paul to stay longer, and Apollos later refutes the Jews in Achaia.

l: Corinth, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: Corinth is where Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, works, and reasons in the synagogue. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believes with his household, and many Corinthians believe and are baptized. The Lord tells Paul he has many people in this city, and Paul stays there a year and six months.

l: Ephesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: Paul comes to Ephesus, leaves Priscilla and Aquila there, and reasons with the Jews in the synagogue. He declines their request to stay longer, saying he must keep the coming feast in Jerusalem but will return if God wills. Apollos later arrives there and is instructed more accurately by Priscilla and Aquila.

l: charge before Gallio, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 18
s: The Jews claim that Paul persuades men to worship God contrary to the law. Gallio says he would bear with them if it were wrong or wicked crime, but since it concerns words, names, and their own law, he refuses to judge it and drives them from the judgment seat.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: Paul arrives at Ephesus and finds about twelve disciples who knew only John's baptism; after he explains and they are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, the Holy Spirit comes on them when he lays hands on them. Paul speaks in the synagogue for three months, then teaches daily in the school of Tyrannus for two years, while God works miracles through him. Seven sons of Sceva fail to exorcise an evil spirit using Jesus's name and flee beaten, which leads to fear, confessions, and the burning of magical books worth fifty thousand pieces of silver. The silversmith Demetrius stirs the craftsmen to anger over the threat to the trade in Artemis shrines, producing a riot in the theater where Gaius and Aristarchus are seized. The town clerk quiets the crowd, tells them to use the courts or regular assembly, warns of the danger of accusation over the riot, and dismisses the assembly.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: Paul comes to Ephesus, explains John's baptism to certain disciples, and lays hands on them so the Holy Spirit comes. He speaks in the synagogue for three months and then in the school of Tyrannus for two years, with special miracles done by his hands, and he determines to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem and then Rome. When the riot breaks out, the disciples and some Asiarchs keep him from entering the theater.

l: Ephesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: Ephesus is where Paul finds the disciples and teaches for about two years, so that all in Asia hear the word. Its people, Jews and Greeks, fear and magnify the name of the Lord Jesus after the exorcists' failure. The town clerk describes the city as temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis and of the image which fell from Zeus.

l: disciples (certain disciples at Ephesus), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: About twelve men, disciples at Ephesus, say they received only John's baptism and have not heard of the Holy Spirit. After Paul's explanation they are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, and when he lays hands on them the Holy Spirit comes and they speak with other languages and prophesy.

l: Holy Spirit, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: The Holy Spirit is something the Ephesian disciples had not heard of. It comes on them when Paul lays hands on them, and they speak with other languages and prophesy. Paul also determines in the Spirit to travel to Jerusalem and then Rome.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: Paul says John told people to believe in the one who would come after him, Christ Jesus. The disciples are baptized in his name, and the exorcists try to invoke him, but the evil spirit says it knows Jesus. After the exorcists' defeat the name of the Lord Jesus is magnified in Ephesus.

l: the Way, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: Some in the synagogue are hardened and speak evil of the Way before the multitude, so Paul separates the disciples. A no small disturbance arises concerning the Way, which leads into Demetrius's complaint and the riot.

l: itinerant Jewish exorcists, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: Some itinerant Jewish exorcists, including seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, try to cast out evil spirits by adjuring them by Jesus whom Paul preaches. The evil spirit answers that it knows Jesus and Paul but not them, and the possessed man overpowers them so they flee naked and wounded.

l: evil spirit, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: An evil spirit answers the exorcists that it knows Jesus and Paul but asks who they are. The man it possessed leaps on the seven, overpowers them, and prevails so that they flee the house naked and wounded. Elsewhere evil spirits go out of the sick when handkerchiefs or aprons from Paul's body are carried to them.

l: burning of magical books, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: After the exorcists' failure, many believers confess their deeds, and many who practiced magical arts bring their books together and burn them in the sight of all. The books are counted as worth fifty thousand pieces of silver, and the word of the Lord grows and becomes mighty.

l: Demetrius, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: Demetrius is a silversmith who makes silver shrines of Artemis and brings no little business to the craftsmen. He gathers them and warns that Paul has persuaded many that gods made with hands are no gods, endangering their trade and the temple and majesty of Artemis.

l: craftsmen, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: The craftsmen and workmen of like occupation are gathered by Demetrius, who reminds them their wealth comes from the shrine business. They fill with anger and cry out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

l: Artemis, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: Artemis is the great goddess of the Ephesians, whom all Asia and the world are said to worship, and whose temple and silver shrines support the trade of Demetrius and the craftsmen. Her majesty is said to be threatened by Paul's teaching, and the crowd cries "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" for about two hours.

l: Ephesian riot, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: The city fills with confusion and the people rush into the theater, seizing Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians and Paul's travel companions. Paul is kept from entering by the disciples and Asiarchs, and most in the assembly do not know why they came. The crowd shouts down Alexander, a Jew, and the town clerk finally quiets it and dismisses the assembly.

l: town clerk, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: The town clerk quiets the multitude and says Ephesus is temple keeper of Artemis, so they should be calm and do nothing rash. He says the men seized are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers, directs Demetrius and the craftsmen to the courts and proconsuls, warns they risk accusation over the riot, and dismisses the assembly.

l: crowd of Ephesians, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19
s: The crowd rushes into the theater in confusion, with most not knowing why they have come. When they perceive that Alexander is a Jew, they cry out for about two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" The town clerk then quiets them and dismisses them.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 20
s: After the uproar, Paul left for Macedonia and Greece, spent three months there, and returned through Macedonia when a plot by Jews threatened him; a group of companions went ahead to Troas. At Troas, a young man named Eutychus fell from a third-floor window while Paul spoke late into the night, and Paul embraced him and declared his life was in him, so he was brought in alive. Paul then traveled by land and ship toward Miletus, bypassing Ephesus because he was hastening to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost. At Miletus he called the Ephesian elders and gave a farewell speech recalling his ministry, warning of coming trials and false teachers, and urging them to shepherd the flock. He knelt and prayed with them, and they wept and accompanied him to the ship, grieved that they would see his face no more.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 20
s: Paul left for Macedonia and Greece, stayed three months, and changed his route to return through Macedonia after a plot by Jews. At Troas he preached until midnight, embraced the fallen Eutychus and said his life was in him, then continued talking until daybreak before departing. He bypassed Ephesus to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, called the Ephesian elders to Miletus, and said he goes bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, where bonds and afflictions await him.

l: Eutychus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 20
s: Eutychus, a young man weighed down with deep sleep, sat in a window at Troas while Paul spoke at length and fell from the third floor, being taken up dead. Paul went down and embraced him, saying his life was in him, and the boy was brought in alive, to the great comfort of those present.

l: Miletus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 20
s: Miletus was where the travelers arrived after sailing past Chios, Samos, and Trogyllium. From there Paul sent to Ephesus for the elders of the assembly and delivered his farewell speech to them. The ship waiting there was where the elders accompanied him at the end.

l: elders of the assembly (Ephesus), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 20
s: The elders were summoned by Paul from Ephesus to Miletus. They were told that the Holy Spirit had made them overseers to shepherd the assembly, that vicious wolves and perverse men from among themselves would arise, and that they would see Paul's face no more. They wept, fell on his neck and kissed him, and accompanied him to the ship.

l: Paul's farewell speech, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 20
s: Paul's speech at Miletus recounts his service in Asia with humility, tears, and trials, his public and house-to-house teaching, and his testimony to Jews and Greeks of repentance and faith. He declares himself clean of all men's blood, warns of wolves and men who will draw disciples away, entrusts the elders to God and the word of his grace, and cites his own labor and the Lord Jesus' saying, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: Paul and his companions sail from Cos and Rhodes to Patara, then Tyre, Ptolemais, and Caesarea, where disciples at Tyre and the prophet Agabus warn that Paul will be bound in Jerusalem. Paul insists he is ready to be bound and even die for the Lord Jesus, and the party goes up to Jerusalem. There James and the elders tell Paul that many believing Jews are zealous for the law and have heard he teaches Jews to forsake Moses, so they urge him to pay for and join four men in a vow and purification. While Paul is in the temple, Jews from Asia stir up the crowd, accusing him of teaching against the people, the law, and the temple and of bringing Greeks in, having seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city. The crowd drags Paul out and tries to kill him, but the commanding officer arrives with soldiers, arrests and chains him, mistakes him for an Egyptian rebel, and finally permits him to address the people in Hebrew from the stairs.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: Paul travels by ship to Tyre, Caesarea, and Jerusalem despite warnings through the Spirit and Agabus that he will be bound, saying he is ready to be bound and to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. In Jerusalem he reports God's work among the Gentiles, follows the elders' advice to undergo purification and pay for four men under a vow, and is seized in the temple, beaten, and chained. He tells the commanding officer he is a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia and is allowed to speak to the people in Hebrew.

l: Paul's companions (we), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: The narrator's group travels with Paul from Cos through Rhodes, Patara, Tyre, Ptolemais, and Caesarea, staying with disciples and with Philip the evangelist. They beg Paul with the local people not to go up to Jerusalem, then cease, saying 'The Lord's will be done,' and go with him to Jerusalem, where the brothers receive them gladly and they meet James.

l: Jerusalem, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: Jerusalem is the destination Paul is warned not to go to, and where the brothers receive him gladly and James and the elders meet him. The whole city is stirred up when Paul is accused in the temple, and the crowd seizes him. Agabus's prophecy that the Jews there would bind him and deliver him to the Gentiles begins to be fulfilled.

l: Agabus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: Agabus, a prophet, comes down from Judea to Caesarea while Paul stays there. He binds his own feet and hands with Paul's belt and declares in the Holy Spirit's name that the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the owner of the belt and deliver him to the Gentiles.

l: Jews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: James and the elders note that many thousands of Jews have believed and are all zealous for the law, and that they have been told Paul teaches Jews among the Gentiles to forsake Moses. Other Jews, from Asia, stir up the multitude against Paul in the temple, and the crowd tries to kill him, fulfilling the prophecy that Jews would bind him.

l: vow and purification, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: The elders propose that Paul join four men who have taken a vow, purify himself with them, and pay their expenses so they may shave their heads, showing that he keeps the law. Paul does so, entering the temple the next day to declare the days of purification until offerings are made for each man. The seven days are almost complete when he is seized.

l: temple, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: Paul enters the temple to carry out the purification, and the Jews from Asia see him there. He is accused of defiling the holy place by bringing Greeks in, and the crowd drags him out and the doors are shut immediately.

l: the Jews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: The Jews from Asia see Paul in the temple, stir up the multitude, and lay hands on him. They cry out that he teaches everywhere against the people, the law, and the place, and that he brought Greeks into the temple, wrongly assuming he had brought Trophimus the Ephesian, whom they had seen with him in the city.

l: crowd, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: The crowd runs together, seizes Paul, drags him out of the temple, and tries to kill him, stopping the beating only when the soldiers appear. Its members shout conflicting things, so the officer cannot learn the truth, and they follow crying 'Away with him!' until Paul gains a great silence by beckoning from the stairs.

l: commanding officer (Claudius Lysias), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: The commanding officer of the regiment hears that Jerusalem is in an uproar and runs down with soldiers and centurions, ending the beating. He arrests Paul, has him bound with two chains, and has him taken toward the barracks, asking whether he is the Egyptian who led four thousand Assassins into the wilderness. After Paul answers, he permits Paul to speak to the people.

l: uproar in Jerusalem and Paul's arrest, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 21
s: After Asian Jews accuse Paul in the temple, all the city is moved and the people seize him and try to kill him. The commanding officer intervenes, has Paul chained, and cannot learn the cause from the shouting, so he orders Paul carried up the stairs by soldiers because of the crowd's violence. Paul is then allowed to address the people.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: In Acts 22, Paul addresses a hostile Jerusalem crowd in Hebrew, describing his upbringing under Gamaliel, his former persecution of the Way, and his encounter with Jesus of Nazareth on the road to Damascus. He recounts being blinded, healed by Ananias, told to be baptized, and later commissioned in a temple trance to go to the Gentiles. The crowd erupts at the mention of the Gentiles and calls for his death. The commanding officer orders Paul scourged in the barracks, but Paul reveals he is a Roman citizen by birth, causing the examiners to withdraw and the officer to fear. The next day the officer releases Paul from his bonds and brings him before the chief priests and council.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: Paul defends himself in Hebrew before the Jerusalem crowd, telling of his Jewish upbringing, his persecution of the Way, and his conversion and commission to the Gentiles. After the crowd demands his death, he is bound for scourging but asserts his Roman citizenship, and the next day he is freed from his bonds and set before the council.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: Jesus of Nazareth identifies himself to Saul in a great light near Damascus, asking why Saul persecutes him and directing him into the city. Later he appears to Paul in a temple trance, telling him to leave Jerusalem because they will not receive his testimony and that he will send him far away to the Gentiles.

l: Ananias, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: Ananias is described as a devout man according to the law, well reported of by all the Jews in Damascus. He comes to the blinded Saul, restores his sight, tells him he is appointed to know God's will and be a witness to all men, and urges him to be baptized and call on the Lord's name.

l: Jerusalem, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: Jerusalem is where Paul speaks to the crowd, where he was raised at Gamaliel's feet, and where he was bound to bring the Damascus believers. It is also where he prayed in the temple and received the vision telling him to leave, and where the crowd demands his death and the officer holds him in the barracks.

l: Damascus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: Damascus is the destination of Paul's journey with letters from the high priest and council to bring believers bound to Jerusalem. On the way a great light and the voice of Jesus stop him, and he enters the city blind, where Ananias restores his sight.

l: Jews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: Jews in Damascus speak well of Ananias, and the Jews are those whom the commanding officer wants to understand as Paul's accusers. Paul presents himself as a Jew, born in Tarsus and zealous for God like his hearers.

l: the crowd (Jerusalem), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: The crowd grows quieter when Paul speaks in Hebrew and listens until he mentions being sent to the Gentiles. They then cry out for him to be removed from the earth as unfit to live, throwing off cloaks and tossing dust into the air.

l: the Way, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: The Way is the movement Paul says he persecuted to the death, binding and imprisoning both men and women. The high priest and council are cited as witnesses to his actions against it.

l: commanding officer (Claudius Lysias), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: The commanding officer has Paul brought into the barracks and orders him examined by scourging to learn why the crowd shouts against him. Upon learning Paul is a Roman, he becomes afraid because he had bound him, and the next day he frees Paul and convenes the chief priests and council.

l: Paul's vision on the road to Damascus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: Paul recounts a noon light from the sky, a voice identifying itself as Jesus of Nazareth, and his companions seeing the light but not understanding the voice. It left him blind, led into Damascus, and began his commission to be a witness to all men.

l: scourging of Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: The commanding officer orders Paul examined by scourging, and Paul is tied with straps. It is halted before it begins when Paul asks whether it is lawful to scourge an uncondemned Roman, and those about to examine him depart.

l: Roman citizenship, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 22
s: Paul invokes his Roman status to challenge the scourging, and the centurion warns the commanding officer. The officer says he bought his citizenship at great price, while Paul says he was born a Roman, and this causes the officer fear for having bound him.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: Paul addresses the council, is struck on the high priest Ananias's order, and rebukes him before apologizing on learning of his office. Paul then declares himself a Pharisee judged over the resurrection of the dead, dividing the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the commanding officer removes him to the barracks for safety. The Lord tells Paul he must testify in Rome, while more than forty Jews bind themselves under a curse to kill him and ask the chief priests and elders to help by requesting that he be brought down to the council. Paul's sister's son learns of the ambush and warns Paul and the commanding officer, who sends Paul by night under heavy military escort to the governor Felix in Caesarea with a letter stating that Paul faces no charge worthy of death or imprisonment. Felix learns Paul is from Cilicia, promises to hear him when his accusers arrive, and orders him kept in Herod's palace.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: Paul tells the council he has lived in good conscience before God, rebukes Ananias after being struck, and apologizes upon learning Ananias is high priest. He declares himself a Pharisee judged over the resurrection, which divides the council, and is rescued by soldiers. The Lord tells him he must testify in Rome; he exposes the plot through his nephew and is taken to Caesarea, where Felix orders him kept in Herod's palace.

l: council, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: The council hears Paul's statement and sees its Pharisee and Sadducee members split into a great argument over the resurrection after Paul speaks. The conspirators plan to have it request Paul's return under the pretense of examining his case more exactly.

l: Pharisees, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: The Pharisees confess the resurrection, angels, and spirits, and Paul identifies himself as a Pharisee and son of Pharisees. Some of their scribes contend they find no evil in Paul and suggest that a spirit or angel may have spoken to him, urging that they not fight against God.

l: commanding officer (Claudius Lysias), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: Fearing Paul would be torn apart, he has soldiers take Paul by force into the barracks. After hearing of the plot from Paul's nephew, he orders two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen to take Paul to Felix by night. He writes a letter identified as from Claudius Lysias saying Paul was accused over questions of the law and not charged with anything worthy of death or imprisonment.

l: Felix, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: Felix, the governor at Caesarea, receives Paul and the letter from Claudius Lysias. He asks Paul's province, learns he is from Cilicia, promises to hear him when his accusers arrive, and commands that he be kept in Herod's palace.

l: the Jews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: More than forty Jews band together and bind themselves under a curse to neither eat nor drink until they have killed Paul. They tell the chief priests and elders to have the commanding officer bring Paul down, planning to kill him before he arrives, but their plan is discovered and Paul is moved out of their reach.

l: young man (Paul's sister's son), The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: Paul's sister's son hears that the conspirators are lying in wait, goes into the barracks, and tells Paul. A centurion brings him to the commanding officer, to whom he reveals the plot and the request the Jews will make. The commanding officer lets him go with a charge to tell no one.

l: plot to kill Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: More than forty men plan an ambush to kill Paul by having the council ask for him to be brought down on the pretense of a more exact inquiry. The plot is revealed by Paul's sister's son, and the commanding officer defeats it by sending Paul away at night to Caesarea under armed escort.

l: resurrection of the dead, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 23
s: Paul says he is being judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead, which sets the Pharisees against the Sadducees. The text explains that the Sadducees deny resurrection, angel, and spirit while the Pharisees confess all of them.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 24
s: Five days after Paul's transfer, the high priest Ananias, some elders, and the orator Tertullus come to the governor Felix and accuse Paul of being a plague, an instigator of insurrections among Jews, a ringleader of the Nazarenes, and of trying to profane the temple. Paul answers that he went to Jerusalem to worship only twelve days earlier, that no one found him disputing or stirring a crowd, and that he serves God according to the Way and hopes in the resurrection of the dead. Felix, who knows the Way well, defers the case until the commanding officer Lysias comes down, and keeps Paul in custody with some privileges. Felix and his wife Drusilla later hear Paul speak about faith in Christ Jesus, and Felix is terrified when Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control, and judgment to come. Felix hopes for a bribe and talks with Paul often, but after two years, when Porcius Festus succeeds him, he leaves Paul in bonds to gain favor with the Jews.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 24
s: Paul is accused before Felix by Tertullus and the Jewish leaders, and defends himself by saying he came to Jerusalem only twelve days earlier to worship and bring gifts and offerings for the needy. He confesses that he serves God according to the Way and hopes in the resurrection, and says he was judged before the council over that one point. He is kept in custody with privileges, speaks to Felix and Drusilla about faith in Christ Jesus, and is left in bonds after two years.

l: Felix, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 24
s: Felix, the governor, hears the accusation against Paul and defers the case until Lysias comes down, having more exact knowledge of the Way. He orders Paul kept in custody with privileges, and is terrified when Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control, and judgment to come. He hopes for money from Paul, and when succeeded by Porcius Festus after two years, leaves Paul in bonds to gain favor with the Jews.

l: Ananias, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 24
s: Ananias, the high priest, comes down after five days with certain elders and the orator Tertullus. Together they inform the governor against Paul.

l: Tertullus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 24
s: Tertullus, an orator, speaks for the accusers, flattering Felix for the peace and prosperity under his foresight. He accuses Paul of being a plague, an instigator of insurrections among Jews throughout the world, a ringleader of the Nazarenes, and one who tried to profane the temple.

l: Jews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 24
s: The Jews join in the attack on Paul, affirming Tertullus's accusations. Paul says certain Jews from Asia, who found him purified in the temple, ought to have appeared before Felix to accuse him. Felix, desiring to gain their favor, leaves Paul in bonds at the end.

l: the Way, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 24
s: The Way is called a sect by Paul's accusers, but Paul confesses that he serves the God of his fathers according to it, believing all that is in the law and the prophets. Felix is said to have more exact knowledge concerning it.

l: resurrection of the dead, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 24
s: Paul states that he hopes toward God for a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust, which his accusers also look for. He says this is the one thing for which he is being judged before the council.

l: Paul's trial before Felix, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 24
s: The hearing opens with the accusation by Ananias, the elders, and Tertullus, followed by Paul's defense denying any disputing, crowd-stirring, or provable charge. Felix defers a decision until Lysias comes down and keeps Paul in custody. The case is never decided, and after two years Felix leaves Paul in bonds when Porcius Festus succeeds him.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: Festus, newly arrived in his province, goes up to Jerusalem, where the high priest and leading Jews ask him to summon Paul there, plotting to kill him on the way. Festus instead holds the hearing at Caesarea, where the Jews bring grievous charges they cannot prove and Paul denies wrongdoing against the Jewish law, the temple, or Caesar. When Festus proposes a trial in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and Festus, after conferring with the council, agrees to send him. King Agrippa and Bernice then arrive, Festus explains the case to Agrippa, and Agrippa asks to hear Paul. Festus brings Paul before Agrippa and the assembled men, saying he found nothing worthy of death and needs something definite to write to the emperor.

l: Festus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: Festus goes up to Jerusalem three days after arriving in the province, refuses the Jews' request to bring Paul there, and hears the case at Caesarea. Seeking to gain favor with the Jews, he asks Paul about being judged in Jerusalem, then sends Paul to Caesar after conferring with the council. He lays the case before King Agrippa and presents Paul to him, wanting something certain to write to the emperor about the charges.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: Paul is kept in custody at Caesarea and, at his hearing, denies having sinned against the Jewish law, the temple, or Caesar. He refuses to be tried in Jerusalem, says he does not refuse to die if guilty, and appeals to Caesar. He is later brought before King Agrippa and the assembled men at Festus's command.

l: Jerusalem, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: Jerusalem is where Festus goes after arriving in the province and stays more than ten days. The high priest and principal Jews there ask him to summon Paul, plotting to kill him on the way. Festus later asks Paul whether he will go there to be judged, and Paul refuses.

l: Caesarea, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: Caesarea is where Paul is kept in custody and where Festus returns after his stay in Jerusalem. Festus sits on the judgment seat there to hear Paul. King Agrippa and Bernice arrive there, and Paul is brought before Agrippa and the others there.

l: the Jews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: The high priest and principal men of the Jews inform Festus against Paul and ask him to summon Paul to Jerusalem, plotting to kill him on the way. They come down to Caesarea and bring many grievous charges they cannot prove. Festus later says the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned him, crying that Paul ought not to live any longer.

l: Caesar, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: Caesar is the authority to whom Paul appeals, saying he is standing before Caesar's judgment seat, and Festus answers that to Caesar he shall go. Paul denies having sinned against Caesar. Festus says he has nothing certain to write to his lord, referring to the emperor.

l: King Agrippa, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: King Agrippa arrives at Caesarea with Bernice and greets Festus. After Festus tells him Paul's case, he says he would like to hear the man himself. The next day he comes with great pomp to the hearing, where Festus addresses him and hopes his examination of Paul will give something to write.

l: Paul's appeal to Caesar, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: When Festus asks whether Paul will go to Jerusalem to be judged, Paul declares that he stands where he ought to be tried and appeals to Caesar. Festus confers with the council and rules that Paul shall go to Caesar. Festus keeps Paul in custody until he can send him.

l: Paul's trial, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: Festus sits on the judgment seat at Caesarea and has Paul brought, while the Jews from Jerusalem stand around him with their charges. Paul gives his defense, and Festus's proposal to move the matter to Jerusalem is rejected by Paul's appeal. Festus later says he has described Roman practice that an accused must meet his accusers face to face, and he arranges a further hearing before Agrippa.

l: charges against Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 25
s: The Jews bring many grievous charges they cannot prove, and Paul denies sinning against the Jewish law, the temple, or Caesar. Festus says they did not charge him with the things he supposed, but only had questions about their own religion and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. Festus found nothing worthy of death and wants to specify the charges when sending Paul.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: Paul, permitted by King Agrippa to speak, makes his defense, describing his early life as a Pharisee, his persecution of those who followed Jesus of Nazareth, and his encounter with a heavenly light and the voice of Jesus on the road to Damascus. He explains that he obeyed the vision by preaching repentance to Jews and Gentiles, and that the Jews seized him in the temple for it. Festus interrupts, calling Paul crazy, but Paul insists he speaks truth and appeals to Agrippa's belief in the prophets. Agrippa asks whether Paul is trying to make him a Christian, and Paul prays that all who hear him might become as he is, except for his bonds. Agrippa, Festus and Bernice withdraw and agree Paul has done nothing worthy of death or bonds, and Agrippa says he could have been freed had he not appealed to Caesar.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: Paul makes his defense before King Agrippa, recounting his Pharisee upbringing, his persecution of the saints, and his conversion and commissioning on the road to Damascus. He says he obeyed the heavenly vision, preached repentance to Jews and Gentiles, and was seized by the Jews in the temple. He rejects Festus's charge of madness, presses Agrippa on his belief in the prophets, and wishes all his hearers might become as he is, except for his bonds.

l: King Agrippa, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: King Agrippa permits Paul to speak and is described as expert in Jewish customs and questions. Paul asks whether he believes the prophets, and Agrippa responds by asking if Paul is trying to make him a Christian. Afterward he tells Festus that Paul might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.

l: Festus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: Festus interrupts Paul's defense with a loud voice, saying Paul is crazy and that great learning is driving him insane. Paul answers him respectfully as most excellent Festus, and Festus later withdraws with the others and hears Agrippa's remark that Paul could have been freed had he not appealed to Caesar.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: Paul says he once believed he should act against the name of Jesus of Nazareth. Paul reports that Jesus spoke to him from the light on the road, identified himself as the one Paul was persecuting, and appointed him a servant and witness to the Jews and Gentiles.

l: the Jews, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: The Jews accuse Paul over the hope of the promise made to their fathers, and Paul says they know his way of life from his youth. He says they seized him in the temple and tried to kill him, and that he was sent to deliver them and the Gentiles from darkness to light.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: Paul says God made a promise to the fathers, which the twelve tribes hope to attain, and that God raises the dead. He credits help from God for his standing to this day and prays that Agrippa and all who hear him might become as he is.

l: Paul's defense, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: Paul's defense before Agrippa covers his Pharisee life, his persecution of the saints, his vision at Damascus, and his preaching of repentance, which he says is nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen. It is interrupted by Festus, and afterward Agrippa, Festus, Bernice and the others agree Paul does nothing worthy of death or bonds.

l: Paul's vision on the road to Damascus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: At noon on the way to Damascus, Paul saw a light from the sky brighter than the sun, and he and his companions fell to the earth. He heard Jesus speak in Hebrew, rebuking his persecution and appointing him a servant and witness to the Gentiles. Paul says he was not disobedient to this vision.

l: resurrection of the dead, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 26
s: Paul asks why it is judged incredible if God raises the dead, and says his accusation concerns the hope of the promise to the fathers. He states that the Christ must suffer and, by the resurrection of the dead, be first to proclaim light to the people and the Gentiles.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 27
s: Paul and other prisoners are handed to the centurion Julius and sail toward Italy, first on a ship of Adramyttium and then on a ship of Alexandria from Myra, with Aristarchus accompanying them. After difficult sailing along Crete, Paul warns that continuing will bring loss, but Julius heeds the master and owner, and the majority choose to sail on from Fair Havens toward Phoenix. The stormy wind Euroclydon drives the ship for many days, the crew jettisons cargo and tackle, and hope is lost until Paul reports an angel's promise that all aboard will live though the ship will be lost. On the fourteenth night, Paul stops the sailors' attempt to flee in the boat, urges everyone to eat, and the 276 people aboard are fed. The ship runs aground where two seas meet and breaks up, Julius prevents the soldiers from killing the prisoners in order to save Paul, and everyone reaches land safely by swimming or on planks.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 27
s: Paul is delivered with other prisoners to the centurion Julius and sails toward Italy, receiving kind treatment at Sidon. He warns that the voyage will bring loss of cargo, ship and lives, is ignored, and later reports an angel's message that he must stand before Caesar and that God has granted him all who sail with him. He tells the centurion that the sailors must stay in the ship, urges all to eat, gives thanks over bread, and is spared when the centurion stops the soldiers from killing the prisoners.

l: Julius, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 27
s: Julius, a centurion of the Augustan band, takes charge of Paul and other prisoners, treats Paul kindly at Sidon, and puts them aboard a ship of Alexandria at Myra. He heeds the master and owner of the ship over Paul's warning, but later acts on Paul's advice about the sailors. Desiring to save Paul, he stops the soldiers from killing the prisoners and orders swimmers to go overboard first.

l: Alexandrian ship, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 27
s: The centurion finds this ship at Myra sailing for Italy and puts Paul and the others on board. It sails slowly past Cnidus and Crete, leaves Fair Havens for Phoenix, and is caught by the Euroclydon wind and driven along. It is reinforced with cables, lightened of cargo, tackle and wheat, and finally runs aground with its bow stuck fast while the stern breaks up in the waves.

l: Euroclydon, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 27
s: Euroclydon is the stormy wind that beats down from shore shortly after a gentle south wind lures the ship along Crete. It catches the ship, which cannot face it, and drives it along for many days without sun or stars, until all hope of being saved is lost.

l: sailors, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 27
s: The sailors, along with the master and owner, are the ones the majority follow in deciding to leave Fair Havens. At midnight on the fourteenth night they sense land, take soundings of twenty and then fifteen fathoms, and drop four anchors from the stern. They try to flee in the boat under the pretense of laying out bow anchors, but Paul exposes this and the soldiers cut the boat away.

l: soldiers, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 27
s: The soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall off after Paul warns that the sailors must stay aboard. When the ship runs aground, they counsel killing the prisoners so none can swim away and escape, but the centurion stops them.

l: people aboard the ship, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 27
s: The 276 people aboard endure the storm, throw cargo and tackle overboard, and go long without food. Encouraged by Paul, they eat, then lighten the ship further by throwing out the wheat. When the ship breaks up, they all reach land safely, some swimming and the rest on planks and other things from the ship.

l: shipwreck on the island, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 27
s: The ship is run aground at a place where two seas meet, after the crew fails to recognize the land but sees a bay with a beach and tries to drive the ship onto it. The bow sticks immovable while the stern breaks up under the waves. This fulfills Paul's prediction that they must run aground on a certain island, and all aboard escape safely to land.

l: The Acts of the Apostles, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 28
s: After escaping the sea, Paul and his companions learn they are on Malta, where the natives show them kindness, Paul survives a viper bite, and he heals the father of the chief man Publius and other sick islanders. After three months they sail in an Alexandrian ship via Syracuse, Rhegium and Puteoli to Rome, where brothers meet them on the way. In Rome Paul, guarded by a soldier, explains to the Jewish leaders why he is a prisoner and testifies about God's Kingdom and Jesus from the law and the prophets. Some believe and some do not, and Paul quotes Isaiah and declares that God's salvation is sent to the nations. He stays two years in his rented house, preaching boldly without hindrance.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 28
s: Paul gathers sticks on Malta, is bitten by a viper, shakes it into the fire and is unharmed, so the natives call him a god. He heals Publius's father and other sick islanders, then travels to Rome, where he is allowed to stay with a guarding soldier. He tells the Jewish leaders he is bound for the hope of Israel, testifies about God's Kingdom and Jesus, quotes Isaiah, and stays two years in his rented house preaching with all boldness and without hindrance.

l: Malta, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 28
s: Malta is the island the escaped party learns they have reached. Its natives show kindness, Publius holds lands there, and the sick of the island are cured; the party stays three months and a ship of Alexandria that had wintered there carries them on.

l: natives of Malta, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 28
s: The natives show uncommon kindness by kindling a fire for the survivors because of the rain and cold. They first take Paul's viper bite as a sign he is a murderer, then call him a god when he is unharmed, and they honor the party and supply their needs when they sail.

l: Rome, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 28
s: Rome is where Paul arrives as a prisoner, delivered by the centurion to the captain of the guard. Brothers come out to meet him as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns, and in the city he meets the Jewish leaders and lives two years in a rented house.

l: Jewish leaders in Rome, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 28
s: Paul calls together the Jewish leaders, and they say they have received no letters or evil reports about him but know the sect is spoken against everywhere. They set a day, hear him from morning till evening, and are divided, some believing and some not. They depart in great dispute after Paul quotes Isaiah about their callous hearts.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 28
s: Paul persuades people concerning Jesus from the law of Moses and the prophets at his lodging in Rome. At the end Paul is said to be teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness.

l: God's Kingdom, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 28
s: Paul explains and testifies about God's Kingdom to the many who come to his lodging in Rome. The chapter ends with him preaching it for two years with all boldness and without hindrance.

l: salvation of God, The Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 28
