s: Paul declares to the Jewish leaders that the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and that they will listen. He says this after quoting Isaiah on a people whose hearts have grown callous.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews / Chapter 1
s: Hebrews chapter 1 says that God, who once spoke to the fathers through the prophets in many times and ways, has now spoken at the end of these days through his Son. The Son is appointed heir of all things, made the worlds, is the radiance of God's glory and the image of his substance, upholds all things by his word, purified us of our sins, and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. The chapter argues that the Son is better than the angels, having inherited a more excellent name. It supports this with a series of quoted statements in which God calls the Son his Son, commands the angels to worship the firstborn, calls the Son God with an eternal throne, and invites him to sit at his right hand. The angels, by contrast, are described as winds and flames of fire and as serving spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews / Chapter 1
s: God spoke to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, and at the end of these days has spoken to us by his Son. He appointed the Son heir of all things and made the worlds through him. He is quoted as calling the Son his Son, commanding the angels to worship the firstborn, addressing the Son as God with an eternal throne, anointing him with the oil of gladness above his fellows, and inviting him to sit at his right hand until the Son's enemies become his footstool.

l: Jesus, The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews / Chapter 1
s: The Son is the one through whom God has spoken at the end of these days, the appointed heir of all things, and the one through whom the worlds were made. He is the radiance of God's glory and the image of his substance, upholds all things by the word of his power, purified us of our sins, and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. He has inherited a name more excellent than the angels', is addressed as God with an eternal throne, is said to have loved righteousness and hated iniquity, is addressed as the Lord who laid the earth's foundation and who remains the same, and is invited to sit at God's right hand until his enemies are made his footstool.

l: angels, The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews / Chapter 1
s: The angels are shown to be lesser than the Son, who has become as much better than they as his inherited name is more excellent than theirs. God never said to any of them "You are my Son" or "Sit at my right hand," and they are commanded to worship the firstborn. They are described as winds and a flame of fire, and as serving spirits sent out to serve those who will inherit salvation.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 urges readers to pay greater attention to what they have heard so they do not drift away, arguing that neglecting so great a salvation, spoken through the Lord and confirmed by those who heard and by God's signs, wonders, and gifts of the Holy Spirit, is more serious than disobeying the word spoken through angels. The world to come was not subjected to angels; a quoted psalm says man was made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory, with all things put under his feet, though this is not yet seen. Jesus, made a little lower than the angels, is crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, tasting death for everyone and being made perfect through sufferings as the author of salvation. Because the children share flesh and blood, Jesus partook of the same so that through death he might bring the devil, who had the power of death, to nothing and free those held in bondage by fear of death. He helps the offspring of Abraham rather than angels, and was made like his brothers to be a merciful and faithful high priest who makes atonement and can help those who are tempted.

l: Jesus, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 2
s: Jesus is the one made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, tasting death for everyone by God's grace. He is the author of salvation made perfect through sufferings, is not ashamed to call those he sanctifies brothers, and shared flesh and blood to bring the devil to nothing. He was made like his brothers to become a merciful and faithful high priest who makes atonement for the people's sins, and having suffered being tempted, he can help those who are tempted.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 2
s: God testified with those who heard the message of salvation by signs, wonders, works of power, and gifts of the Holy Spirit according to his will. All things are for him and through him, and he is bringing many children to glory by making the author of their salvation perfect through sufferings. The children are described as those whom God has given to Jesus.

l: angels, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 2
s: Angels spoke a word that proved steadfast, with every transgression receiving a just penalty. The world to come was not subjected to them, and man and Jesus are described as made a little lower than them. Jesus does not give help to angels but to the offspring of Abraham.

l: offspring of Abraham, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 2
s: The offspring of Abraham are those to whom Jesus gives help, in contrast to angels, who are not helped. This is the reason he was made like his brothers in all things.

l: man (humanity), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 2
s: Quoting a psalm, the text says man was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor, and had all things put under his feet, though not yet seen so. The children, as humanity, share flesh and blood, were subject to bondage through fear of death, and are brought to glory through Jesus, who tasted death for everyone.

l: devil, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 2
s: The devil is identified as the one who had the power of death. Jesus partook of flesh and blood so that through death he might bring the devil to nothing.

l: salvation, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 2
s: Salvation is called so great that neglecting it leaves no escape. It was first spoken through the Lord and confirmed by those who heard, with God testifying by signs, wonders, works of power, and gifts of the Holy Spirit. Jesus is its author, made perfect through sufferings.

l: death, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 2
s: Death is something Jesus tasted for everyone by God's grace, and it is the means by which he brings the devil, who had its power, to nothing. Fear of death had kept people in bondage all their lifetime until Jesus delivered them.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 urges the holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, to consider Jesus, the Apostle and High Priest of their confession, who was faithful to God who appointed him just as Moses was faithful in all his house. Jesus is counted worthy of more glory than Moses because he who built the house has more honor than the house; Moses was a servant in the house, while Christ is a Son over it, and believers are his house if they hold fast their confidence. Quoting the Holy Spirit's words about 'Today if you will hear his voice,' the chapter recalls how the fathers rebelled, tested God in the wilderness for forty years, displeased him, and were sworn not to enter his rest. The readers are warned against an evil heart of unbelief, told to exhort one another daily so they are not hardened by sin's deceitfulness, and reminded that they are partakers of Christ if they hold firm to the end. The chapter concludes that those who came out of Egypt under Moses, who sinned and were disobedient, could not enter the rest because of unbelief.

l: Jesus, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: Jesus is called the Apostle and High Priest of the readers' confession and is to be considered by them. He was faithful to God who appointed him and is counted worthy of more glory than Moses, being faithful as a Son over God's house.

l: Moses, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: Moses was faithful in all God's house as a servant, as a testimony of things to be spoken afterward. He is shown to have less glory than Jesus, and he led the people who came out of Egypt, many of whom rebelled.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: God appointed Jesus and is the one who built all things. He was displeased for forty years with the wilderness generation that tested him, and swore in wrath that they would not enter his rest.

l: house (God's house), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: The house is the one in which Moses was faithful as a servant and over which Christ is faithful as a Son. Its builder has more honor than the house, and the text says 'we are his house' if we hold fast our confidence and the glorying of our hope firm to the end.

l: readers (the audience addressed), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: The readers are addressed as holy brothers and partakers of a heavenly calling, told to consider Jesus. They are warned against an evil heart of unbelief and falling away, urged to exhort one another daily, and told they are partakers of Christ if they hold their confidence firm to the end.

l: those who heard and disobeyed (the Israelites), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: These are the fathers who came out of Egypt led by Moses, heard and rebelled, tested God, and saw his deeds for forty years. God was displeased with them because they erred in their heart and did not know his ways; their bodies fell in the wilderness, and they could not enter his rest because of unbelief.

l: rest (God's rest), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: God's rest is what he swore in wrath that the disobedient wilderness generation would not enter. The chapter states they were unable to enter because of unbelief.

l: rebellion and trial in the wilderness, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: This is the time when the fathers tested and tried God for forty years, even while seeing his deeds. It is cited from the Holy Spirit's words as a warning not to harden hearts, and it was carried out by those who came out of Egypt under Moses.

l: unbelief, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 3
s: Unbelief is warned against as an evil heart that leads to falling away from the living God. It is identified as the reason the wilderness generation could not enter God's rest.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 urges its readers to fear falling short of the promise of entering God's rest. It explains that those who first heard the good news did not profit because they lacked faith and disobeyed, while believers do enter that rest. Citing God's rest on the seventh day and David's "Today" passage, it argues that a Sabbath rest still remains for God's people, since Joshua did not give the rest meant. It describes the word of God as living, active, and able to discern the heart, and closes by presenting Jesus, the Son of God, as a great high priest who sympathizes with human weakness and by encouraging believers to approach the throne of grace.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 4
s: God swore in wrath that those who disobeyed would not enter his rest, and he rested on the seventh day from all his works. Through David he set a certain day, "today", for hearing his voice, and all creatures are open to his sight and must give an account to him.

l: Jesus, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 4
s: Jesus is called a great high priest, the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens. He has been tempted in all points as believers are, yet without sin, so he can be touched with the feeling of their infirmities.

l: rest (God's rest), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 4
s: God's rest is something the believing enter, although God's works were finished from the foundation of the world and he rested on the seventh day. Joshua did not give it, so a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and whoever enters it rests from their own works as God did from his.

l: readers (addressees of the letter), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 4
s: Believers are said to enter that rest and are urged to fear falling short, to give diligence to enter it, and to avoid the example of disobedience. They are told to hold tightly to their confession and to draw near with boldness to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace for help in time of need.

l: those who heard and disobeyed (the Israelites), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 4
s: Those to whom the good news was preached before failed to enter God's rest because of disobedience. The word they heard did not profit them because it was not mixed with faith, and God swore in his wrath that they would not enter his rest.

l: the word of God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 4
s: The word of God is described as living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the dividing of soul and spirit, joints and marrow. It is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 describes the role of a high priest, who is taken from among men to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, can deal gently with the ignorant because he shares their weakness, and must offer sacrifices for himself as well as the people. No one takes this honor on himself; he is called by God, as Aaron was. Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest but was named so by God, who called him Son and a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. In the days of his flesh Christ prayed with strong crying and tears, was heard for his godly fear, learned obedience through suffering, and, made perfect, became the author of eternal salvation to those who obey him. The writer then rebukes the readers as dull of hearing, still needing milk rather than solid food, and says solid food belongs to the full grown who have trained their senses to discern good and evil.

l: Christ, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 5
s: Christ did not glorify himself to become a high priest; God said to him, "You are my Son. Today I have become your father," and called him a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. In the days of his flesh he offered prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears, was heard for his godly fear, and though a Son learned obedience by what he suffered. Having been made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation to all who obey him, named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 5
s: God calls the high priest to his office, as he called Aaron, and no one takes the honor on himself. God told Christ, "You are my Son," and declared him a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, naming him high priest. He was also able to save Christ from death and heard Christ's prayers for his godly fear.

l: high priest, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 5
s: Every high priest is taken from among men and appointed for men in things pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. Because he is himself surrounded with weakness, he can deal gently with the ignorant and those going astray, and he must offer sacrifices for his own sins as well as the people's. He does not take the honor himself but is called by God, as Aaron was.

l: recipients (the readers addressed), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 5
s: The readers are described as having become dull of hearing, so that there are many hard-to-interpret words to say about Christ. Although by now they should be teachers, they need someone to teach them again the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. They have come to need milk and not solid food.

l: milk and solid food (spiritual teaching), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 5
s: Milk stands for the elementary teaching suited to babies, and everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness. Solid food is for the full grown, who by use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil. The readers are said to need milk rather than solid food.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: The author urges readers to leave behind the first principles of Christ, such as repentance, faith, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, and judgment, and press on to perfection. He warns that those who were enlightened and partook of the Holy Spirit but fell away cannot be renewed to repentance, and illustrates this with land that bears either a crop and blessing or thorns and a curse. He then tells the beloved readers he is persuaded of better things for them, since God will not forget their work serving the saints, and urges them to persevere like those who inherited the promises. He cites God's promise and oath to Abraham as two immutable things that give strong encouragement, and describes hope as an anchor of the soul that reaches within the veil, where Jesus entered as forerunner and high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: God is said to permit the readers' progress, to bless land that bears good crops, and to be not unrighteous in forgetting their work and love toward his name. He made a promise to Abraham and, swearing by himself since no one was greater, confirmed it with an oath, showing the immutability of his counsel; it is impossible for him to lie.

l: Jesus, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: Jesus is described as having entered within the veil as a forerunner for the readers. He has become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

l: Abraham, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: Abraham received God's promise, "Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you." Having patiently endured, he obtained the promise.

l: those who fell away (once enlightened), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: They were once enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, became partakers of the Holy Spirit, and tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come. Having fallen away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance, since they crucify the Son of God for themselves again and put him to open shame.

l: readers (addressees of the letter), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: The author is persuaded of better things for them, things that accompany salvation, though he warns them sternly. God will not forget their work and labor of love in serving the saints, and they are urged to show diligence to the end and imitate those who inherited the promises through faith and perseverance.

l: land (parable of the land), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: The land drinks the rain that comes often on it. If it produces a suitable crop it receives blessing from God, but if it bears thorns and thistles it is rejected, near being cursed, and its end is to be burned.

l: first principles of Christ, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: These are to be left behind as the readers press on to perfection, without laying the foundation again. They include repentance from dead works, faith toward God, the teaching of baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.

l: God's promise and oath to Abraham, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: God promised Abraham blessing and multiplication and swore by himself since he could swear by no one greater. The promise and oath are two immutable things in which God cannot lie, giving strong encouragement to those who have fled for refuge to take hold of the hope set before them.

l: hope, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 6
s: Hope is described as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, entering into that which is within the veil. It is set before those who have fled for refuge, and the readers are urged to show diligence toward the fullness of hope to the end.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 7
s: Chapter 7 argues that Jesus' priesthood is superior to the Levitical priesthood by way of Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who met Abraham, blessed him, and received a tenth from him. Because the lesser is blessed by the greater, and because Levi was figuratively in Abraham when he paid tithes, the text concludes that Melchizedek's priesthood surpasses that of Levi. Since perfection did not come through the Levitical priesthood, a priest of another order arose from Judah, which changes the law and annuls a former commandment because of its weakness. Jesus was made priest with an oath, lives forever, and so holds an unchangeable priesthood, able to save completely those who draw near to God through him. Unlike the high priests who offer daily sacrifices for their own sins and the people's, he offered himself once for all, and is appointed as a Son perfected forever.

l: Melchizedek, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 7
s: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, blessed him, and received a tenth from him. His name is interpreted as king of righteousness and king of peace, and he is described as without father, mother, or genealogy, with neither beginning of days nor end of life, made like the Son of God and remaining a priest continually. He is shown to be greater than Abraham because he blessed him.

l: Abraham, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 7
s: Abraham, the patriarch, gave Melchizedek a tenth of the best plunder and was blessed by him, which shows that Abraham, who has the promises, is the lesser. Levi, still in the body of his father Abraham, is said to have paid tithes through him.

l: Jesus, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 7
s: Jesus is the Lord who sprang out of Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priesthood, and he was made priest after the power of an endless life and with an oath. He has become the guarantee of a better covenant, lives forever with an unchangeable priesthood, and is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him. He is holy, guiltless, undefiled, separated from sinners and higher than the heavens, and is the Son perfected forever.

l: Levitical priesthood, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 7
s: The sons of Levi who receive the priest's office have a commandment to take tithes from their brothers according to the law, but they die and are hindered from continuing. Perfection did not come through it, so another priest was needed, and it is shown to be inferior to Melchizedek's priesthood. Its high priests have weakness and must offer sacrifices daily, first for their own sins.

l: first covenant, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 7
s: The law gave the people the Levitical priesthood and commanded tithes, but it made nothing perfect. Because the priesthood has changed, the law must change too, and a foregoing commandment is annulled for its weakness and uselessness. It appoints men with weakness as high priests, while the later word of the oath appoints a perfected Son forever.

l: tithes, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 7
s: The Levites take tithes from their brothers according to the law, yet Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek. This is used to show Melchizedek's superiority, since those who die receive tithes in one case while in the other one receives them of whom it is testified that he lives. Levi is said to have paid tithes through Abraham.

l: priesthood of Melchizedek order, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 7
s: This priesthood is the one named in the testimony 'You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek,' and it is based on the power of an endless life, not a fleshly commandment. It was established with an oath, unlike the Levitical priests, and it replaces the Aaronic order as the way to a better hope through which people draw near to God. Jesus holds it unchangeably because he lives forever.

l: sacrifice (Jesus' offering of himself), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 7
s: Jesus, the fitting high priest, does not need to offer sacrifices daily as the other high priests do, first for their own sins and then for the people's. He did this once for all when he offered up himself.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 8
s: Chapter 8 states that the main point is that believers have a high priest who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens, serving in the true tabernacle pitched by the Lord, not by man. Because every high priest must offer gifts and sacrifices, this high priest must also have something to offer, and he would not be a priest on earth, where priests serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things according to the law, as Moses was warned to follow the pattern shown on the mountain. The high priest has obtained a more excellent ministry as mediator of a better covenant founded on better promises. Finding fault with the first covenant, the Lord promises through a quoted passage a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, unlike the one made with their fathers when he led them out of Egypt, in which he will put his laws in their minds, write them on their hearts, and be merciful to their unrighteousness and remember their sins no more. By calling it new, the text concludes, he has made the first covenant obsolete and near to vanishing away.

l: the Lord, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 8
s: The Lord pitched the true tabernacle, not man. Finding fault with the first covenant, he declares through the quoted passage that he will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, put his laws in their minds and hearts, be their God, be merciful to their unrighteousness, and remember their sins no more. He also says he disregarded their fathers because they did not continue in his covenant.

l: greater and more perfect tabernacle (heavenly), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 8
s: The true tabernacle is the sanctuary in which the high priest serves, and it was pitched by the Lord, not by man. The earthly priests' service is only a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, as Moses was told to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown on the mountain.
